seoTitle: Change the Canvas Background Color in Power BI
metaDescription: Change a Power BI report's canvas background color: where the setting hides, why a freshly picked color can look invisible, and the Export-to-PDF catch with Wallpaper.
intro: A default white canvas works fine, but changing the background color is one of the fastest ways to make a Power BI report feel intentional instead of generic. The setting takes seconds to apply once you know where it lives, but a default that Microsoft sets on every new report can make a freshly chosen color look like nothing happened. This guide covers where the canvas background option sits, how to apply a color, and the transparency and wallpaper details most people never open.

steps.heading: Start from a plain report page
steps.body: A typical Power BI page before any background styling: white canvas, a few KPI cards at the top, a couple of bar charts below. It reads fine, but every default Power BI report looks the same, which matters if you're presenting next to other people's dashboards. Changing the background is the fastest way to make a report visually distinct without touching a single visual.

image.caption: A standard report page on the default white canvas — KPI cards and bar charts with no background styling applied yet.

steps.heading: Select the canvas and open the Format icon
steps.body: Click empty space on the report canvas, not a visual, then choose the Format icon in the Visualizations pane on the right. With nothing selected, this pane switches to page-level formatting, and Canvas background and Wallpaper appear as separate cards. Canvas background controls the report page itself. Wallpaper controls the gray area outside it, sitting behind the page. Mixing up the two is the most common reason people can't find the setting they want.

image.caption: The Format pane with Canvas background and Wallpaper listed as separate sections.

steps.heading: Open Canvas background and choose a color
steps.body: Expand the Canvas background card and select the Color dropdown to open a full palette: theme colors across the top, tints and shades below, and a Recent colors row for whatever this report has already used. Stick to the theme color row to keep the background coordinated with your chart colors, since those swatches are pulled from the same theme instead of a separate palette.

image.caption: The Canvas background color picker open, showing theme colors, tints and shades, and a Recent colors row.

steps.heading: Check the applied color against its default transparency
steps.body: Once you pick a color the canvas updates: in this example a soft lavender replaces the white, and visual containers stay white by contrast, keeping charts readable against the colored backdrop. Microsoft's documentation notes that every new report sets Canvas background transparency to 100% by default. That default is why a color you just picked can still look like plain white. Drag the Transparency slider down from 100% to make the color visible, then raise it again later if a fully saturated background feels heavy on a real report.

image.caption: The same report page with a lavender canvas background applied. Visual containers stay white, keeping the charts legible against the color.

steps.heading: Try wallpaper, then keep it consistent
steps.body: The Wallpaper card sits below Canvas background with its own Color and Transparency controls, plus an Add file button for a background image behind the page. Wallpaper sits furthest back, so keep any image low-contrast; a busy image competing with your charts defeats the point of adding one. Apply whatever you settle on to every page in the report, not just the one you're testing: a background that changes page to page reads as unfinished. Favor muted, low-saturation colors over bright ones. The background's job is to frame the data, not compete with it.

troubleshooting.problem: The canvas still looks white after picking a new color
troubleshooting.cause: New reports set the Canvas background's transparency to 100% by default, so a color is assigned but invisible until the transparency is lowered.
troubleshooting.fix: Open the Canvas background card and drag the Transparency slider down from 100%. The color appears immediately.

troubleshooting.problem: White text disappears when a report with a colored or image wallpaper is exported to PDF
troubleshooting.cause: Power BI's Export to PDF feature does not include wallpaper, so a wallpaper-only background is dropped and white or very light text loses its backdrop.
troubleshooting.fix: Use Canvas background rather than Wallpaper on a report you plan to export to PDF, or keep text dark enough to stay readable on a plain white page.

troubleshooting.problem: A dotted line appears around the page while editing a high-transparency background
troubleshooting.cause: Power BI adds this border automatically once Canvas background transparency passes 50%, as a guide to the page boundary during editing.
troubleshooting.fix: Ignore it. It's an editing-only aid and does not appear for anyone viewing the published report.

faq.question: Where do I find canvas background settings in Power BI?
faq.answer: Click empty space on the report canvas, then open the Format icon in the Visualizations pane. Canvas background and Wallpaper appear there as separate cards.

faq.question: Why doesn't the canvas change color when I pick one?
faq.answer: New reports set Canvas background transparency to 100% by default. Lower the Transparency slider after choosing a color to actually see it.

faq.question: Can I use an image instead of a solid color?
faq.answer: Yes. The Wallpaper card sits below Canvas background and has its own Add file button and transparency control, independent of the solid-color option.

faq.question: Does a wallpaper image survive PDF export?
faq.answer: No. Microsoft's documentation states that Export to PDF does not include wallpaper, so plan for that if you're relying on light text over a colored background.

faq.question: Should the background be the same on every page of my report?
faq.answer: Generally yes. Keeping the canvas background consistent across pages makes a multi-page report feel like one document instead of several unrelated dashboards.
